title: Brenton’s Greek has a further verse after 7:1: “honour the Lord and you will be strong; fear no other besides him”
summary: The KJV of Proverbs 7:1 is followed directly by 7:2 (“Keep my commandments, and live”). Brenton’s Greek prints a verse labelled 7:1a between them that tells the son to honour the Lord and fear no other.
text: KJV Proverbs 7:1: “My son, keep my words, and lay up my commandments with thee.” KJV Proverbs 7:2: “Keep my commandments, and live; and my law as the apple of thine eye.” Hebrew (WLC) 7:1: בְּ֭נִי שְׁמֹ֣ר אֲמָרָ֑י וּ֝מִצְוֹתַ֗י תִּצְפֹּ֥ן אִתָּֽךְ׃. Brenton’s Greek 7:1: Υἱὲ φύλασσε ἐμοὺς λόγους, τὰς δὲ ἐμὰς ἐντολὰς κρύψον παρὰ σεαυτῷ. Brenton’s Greek 7:1a: Υἱὲ τίμα τὸν Κύριον καὶ ἰσχύσεις, πλὴν δὲ αὐτοῦ μὴ φοβοῦ ἄλλον· [My son, honour the Lord and you will be strong; and besides him fear no other]. Brenton’s Greek 7:2: φύλαξον ἐμὰς ἐντολὰς καὶ βιώσεις, τοὺς δὲ ἐμοὺς λόγους ὥσπερ κόρας ὀμμάτων. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/20/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PRO07.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has no verse of this number. The Greek 7:1a reads Υἱὲ τίμα τὸν Κύριον καὶ ἰσχύσεις, πλὴν δὲ αὐτοῦ μὴ φοβοῦ ἄλλον. The KJV’s verses 7:1–2 command keeping the words and commandments; they do not tell the son to honour the Lord or to fear no other.
scope: T applies at the verse printed as 7:1a in Brenton’s Greek; the KJV number nearest to it is 7:1. The statement about the KJV is limited to Proverbs 7:1–2 as printed. It is not a claim about what the KJV says anywhere else in the Bible or in the book of Proverbs, and the record does not say the added verse contradicts the KJV. The Hebrew has no verse of this label. This compares the wording of the texts quoted. It does not show which wording is original. The book is verse and aphorism; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the writer meant beyond the words quoted. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek quoted is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original, and the record does not claim the Greek is a mistranslation of the Hebrew. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
